classification_signals: The paper describes an experiment with 20 participants (Section 3.1, p. 8).
It details experimental stimuli (19 images of classroom environments) and procedures (Section 3.2, 3.3, p. 8-10).
EEG data was collected using a DSI-24 system and analyzed using statistical tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (Section 3.4, p. 11).
Quantitative results are presented in tables (Table 3, 4, 5, 6, 7) and text, including p-values and effect sizes (Z values) (Section 4, p. 11-17).
The study includes a 'Research Methods' section (Section 3, p. 7) and 'Results' section (Section 4, p. 11).

limitations: The study used rendered images, which may differ from the experience in actual spaces.
The experiment used a monitor instead of a virtual reality head-mounted display due to concerns about discomfort and potential brainwave interference.
The small number of participants (N = 20) limits the generalizability of the results.

Brain and subjective responses were measured, but specific tasks involving concentration and creativity were not used, making it uncertain if people actually perform better in classrooms with revealed stimuli characteristics.
Subjective responses were collected by asking participants to choose the most supportive classroom, rather than using scale ratings for all stimuli, preventing within-subject correlation analysis.
EEGs only measure surface brain activity and do not show deeper brain activity (e.g., amygdala).
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study investigated how various indoor environmental elements (space shape, furniture arrangement, ceiling height, color, and view of nature) influence human brainwave responses related to concentration (Concentration Index, CI) and creativity (Relative Theta, RT), as well as subjective self-reported preferences. Key findings indicate that CI was associated with rectilinear shapes, traditional furniture arrangements, and red walls, while RT was linked to curvilinear shapes, collaborative furniture arrangements, white walls, and natural views. Subjective responses showed alignment with brain responses for furniture layout and shape, but diverged on color preferences. Limitations include the use of rendered images, a small sample size, and the absence of specific performance tasks, suggesting a need for future research with more diverse methods and larger samples to fully understand the complex interplay between environmental design and cognitive functions.
